Official Week 8 Objectives

1. Differentiate Gram-positive from Gram-negative bacteria.
2. Explain Gram stain theory and technique.
3. Identify basic structural features of bacteria.
4. Explain how bacteria divide.
5. Discuss how bacterial spores resist destruction.
6. Outline the biochemical composition of peptidoglycan.
Assigned ScholarRx
Prokaryote Structure and the Gram Stain
How to study this lecture
Shape tells you what you are looking at; structure tells you how it behaves; the cell wall explains Gram staining and drug access; spores explain survival.

Slides 2-15: Prokaryotes, Size, Shape & Arrangement

Slide 3. Prokaryote vs eukaryote overview. The bacterial chromosome is in a cytoplasmic nucleoid, most bacteria have a cell wall, and bacterial respiration occurs at the cell membrane rather than mitochondria.
Core prokaryote picture
No membrane-bound nucleus • nucleoid chromosome • bacterial ribosomes • most have cell wall • cell membrane performs key metabolic functions.
Handout-only clinical connection: bacterial ribosomes are 70S = 30S + 50S, compared with cytosolic human 80S ribosomes. The handout connects this difference to selective antibiotic targeting by classes such as aminoglycosides and macrolides. It also emphasizes that bacterial membranes usually lack sterols, with Mycoplasma as the classic exception.
Slide 7. Three broad shapes in the deck: coccus, bacillus, and spiral.
MorphologyDeck recognition
CoccusSpherical/berry-like
BacillusRod-shaped
SpiralCoiled/helical morphology
Slide 8. Coccal groupings reflect planes of cell division: chains are streptococcal arrangements; grape-like clusters are staphylococcal arrangements.
Slide 9. Direct microscopy comparison of streptococcal chains versus staphylococcal clusters.
Arrangement shortcut
Staph = clusters • Strep = chains. Arrangement is a morphology clue, not a full species diagnosis.
Slide 10. Bacilli divide across the short axis and therefore show fewer classic grouping patterns than cocci.
Slide 12. Corynebacterium diphtheriae is used as the deck example of club- or dumbbell-shaped bacilli.
Slide 13. Vibrio cholerae is the curved/comma-shaped bacillus example.
Slide 14. Spirilla are rigid helical organisms with polar flagella; examples include H. pylori, Campylobacter jejuni, and Spirillum minus.
Slide 15. Spirochetes are helical but have a non-rigid wall and flagella beneath an external sheath; examples include Borrelia, Leptospira, and Treponema.
Spirillum vs spirochete: the lecture distinguishes them by rigidity and flagellar location. Spirilla = rigid helix + polar flagella. Spirochetes = flexible/non-rigid + axial filaments beneath an external sheath.

Slides 16-19: Special Bacterial Forms

Slide 17. Ehrlichia and Anaplasma are shown reproducing within intracellular morulae; the deck labels the monocyte-vs-granulocyte associations.
Slide 18. Chlamydia/Chlamydophila are shown as coccoid Gram-negative nonmotile organisms with elementary and reticulate-body forms.
Slide 19. The current slide labels Mycoplasma as a very small bacterium without a cell wall and shows filamentous growth on agar.
Deck wording note: this companion preserves the instructor slide wording for special organisms rather than silently substituting outside microbiology detail. For course study, know the visual/structural distinctions the deck emphasizes: intracellular forms, elementary/reticulate bodies, and the lack of a cell wall in Mycoplasma.
Handout-only clinical enrichment: Mycoplasma has no cell wall and stabilizes its membrane with host-derived sterols, so beta-lactam cell-wall agents such as penicillin are ineffective. The handout also contrasts Mycobacterium, which has a waxy mycolic-acid-rich envelope and is identified with an acid-fast stain rather than a routine Gram stain.

Slides 20-31, 41-42, 55-56: Basic Bacterial Structures

Flagella = motility

Slide 21. Flagella are composed of flagellin and form a hollow protein cylinder; the lecture emphasizes bacterial motility.
Flagellum anatomy
Filament → hook → basal body. The basal body anchors the flagellum in the cell envelope.

Fimbriae = adherence

Slide 25. Fimbriae form a fringe-like surface and mediate adherence to surfaces, target cells, and other bacteria.
Fimbriae = stick. They are an adherence structure, not the primary motility structure.

Sex pili = DNA transfer interface

Slide 27. The deck identifies F pili / sex pili as fertility-factor structures in Gram-negative organisms.

Glycocalyx = protection + attachment + biofilm

Slide 29. The glycocalyx or sugar coat resists phagocytosis by covering PAMPs and helps attachment. The deck notes most capsules are polysaccharide, with B. anthracis as a protein exception.
Slide 30. A looser slime layer protects against drying, nutrient loss, and chemical insults and is a precursor to mature biofilm.
Slide 31. Biofilm sequence in the deck: colonization → adsorption to surface → glycocalyx production → mature biofilm.
StructureDeck function
FlagellaMotility
FimbriaeAdherence
F/sex piliFertility/conjugation structure
Capsule / glycocalyxAnti-phagocytic shielding + adherence
Slime layerLoose attachment, protection, biofilm precursor
70S ribosome30S + 50S bacterial ribosomal subunits
Handout-only clinical connections:
  • Plasmids are small circular extrachromosomal DNA molecules that commonly carry antibiotic-resistance or virulence genes and can move between bacteria during conjugation.
  • Fimbriae mediate adherence to host surfaces; the handout uses Neisseria gonorrhoeae adherence as an example.
  • The sex pilus is specialized for DNA transfer.
  • The capsule is organized and antiphagocytic, while a slime layer is looser and promotes attachment/biofilm formation.
  • The flagellar basal-body motor is powered by a proton gradient.
Slide 41. Bacterial cell membrane is the site of respiration in the deck: electron transport generates proton motive force that powers ATP synthase.
Slide 56. Bacterial ribosome: 30S small subunit + 50S large subunit = 70S complete ribosome.

Slides 32-40: Cell Wall, Peptidoglycan & Gram Architecture

Slide 33. Big-picture comparison: Gram-positive bacteria have thick peptidoglycan and one membrane; Gram-negative bacteria have a thin peptidoglycan layer plus two membranes.
FeatureGram-positiveGram-negative
PeptidoglycanThickThin
MembranesOne cytoplasmic membraneInner + outer membrane
Teichoic acidsPresentAbsent
LPSAbsentOuter membrane
PorinsNot the defining featureOuter-membrane channels
PeriplasmNot emphasized as a large compartmentPresent
Slide 34. Gram-positive cell wall image: thick peptidoglycan with wall teichoic acid and lipoteichoic acid over the cytoplasmic membrane.
Slide 35. Peptidoglycan chemistry: alternating NAG and NAM glycan chains with peptide side chains and cross-links.
Peptidoglycan formula
NAG + NAM sugar backbone + peptide side chains/cross-linking. The deck lists L-alanine, glutamic acid, lysine, and D-alanine in the peptide component.
Handout-only drug connection: transpeptidase enzymes, also called penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs), cross-link adjacent peptidoglycan strands. Beta-lactam antibiotics inhibit PBPs, weakening the wall and promoting bacterial lysis.
Slide 37. Teichoic acids are negatively charged and only in Gram-positive bacteria; the deck emphasizes ion homeostasis and binding/channel functions.
Slide 39. Gram-negative envelope: outer membrane, LPS, porins, periplasmic space, thin peptidoglycan, and inner membrane.
Slide 40. Porins are trimeric outer-membrane channels that admit small hydrophilic solutes and can exclude larger molecules.
Gram-negative barrier logic
Outer membrane + porins = an extra permeability barrier. The slide visually contrasts a smaller penicillin molecule with the much larger vancomycin molecule.
Handout-only LPS breakdown: Gram-negative LPS contains O antigen for serotyping, a core polysaccharide, and Lipid A, the toxic endotoxin moiety. The handout links Lipid A recognition through TLR4 to IL-1, IL-6, and TNF-alpha release, producing fever, hypotension, and potentially DIC/septic shock. For Gram-positive organisms, the handout highlights lipoteichoic acid as an inflammatory PAMP.

Slides 44-54: Gram Stain Theory, Technique & Morphologic Reading

Slide 45. Gram stain sequence: crystal violet → iodine mordant → alcohol/acetone decolorization → safranin counterstain.
Gram stain order
Crystal violet → iodine → decolorizer → safranin.
StepRole
Crystal violetPrimary stain
Gram iodineMordant; deepens/stabilizes the dye complex
Acetone-alcoholDecolorizer; key differential step
SafraninCounterstain
Ozzy checkpoint - click him once you can predict what over- or under-decolorization does to a smear.
Why Gram-positive stays purple: the deck's assessment item ties retention of the crystal-violet/iodine complex during decolorization to greater peptidoglycan content.
Technique trap: too little decolorizer can make everything look Gram-positive; too much decolorizer can make everything look Gram-negative. The deck tests these errors using neutrophil nuclear staining as a clue.
Slide 46. Gram-positive cocci morphology: clusters (Staphylococcus), chains (Streptococcus), and tetrads (Micrococcus).
Slide 48. Gram-positive bacilli: thick Clostridium-type rods, thin Listeria-type rods, and branched Actinomyces-type forms.
Slide 49. Neisseria gonorrhoeae shown as Gram-negative diplococci in urethral exudate.
Slide 50. Gram-negative rod morphology: elongate Fusobacterium vs shorter rods such as E. coli, Klebsiella, and Pseudomonas.
Slide 54. Haemophilus influenzae demonstrates that organisms may appear coccoid or coccobacillary.
Read a Gram stain in two passes
1) Color: positive or negative. 2) Morphology/arrangement: cocci vs rods, chains vs clusters, diplococci, coccobacilli, branching.

Slides 36 & 43: Bacterial Division

Slide 36. Division-site biology: chromosome replication/separation, Fts proteins at the divisome, Z-ring formation, and new peptidoglycan synthesis.
FtsZ
FtsZ is the key Z-ring protein in the lecture. The Z ring constricts at the division site while new cell-wall material is synthesized.
Deck wording: slide 36 describes “Fts Z → polymerizes into tubulin → constricting Z ring.” This companion preserves the slide's tested association: FtsZ = Z-ring / divisome / bacterial division.
Binary fission: replicate the single bacterial chromosome → segregate copies → septum/cell-wall synthesis → divide into daughter cells.
Handout-only sequence detail: the cell elongates and replicates its circular chromosome, chromosome copies move apart, FtsZ assembles into the central Z-ring, the ring constricts with septum/cell-wall formation, and two daughter cells separate. The handout explicitly calls FtsZ a bacterial homolog of eukaryotic tubulin.

Slides 57-63: Bacterial Spores

Slide 58. Released endospore survival message: spores tolerate extreme heat, lack of water, toxic chemicals, and radiation.
Why spores matter
Endospores are survival structures, not a reproductive multiplication strategy. They allow persistence through otherwise lethal environmental stress.
Slide 60. Early sporulation: chromosome replicates and extends into an axial filament; an asymmetric septum separates forespore from mother cell.
Slide 61. Mother cell engulfs the forespore, surrounding it with a second membrane.
Slide 62. Forespore develops peptidoglycan between the two membranes, calcium is added to the core, and the mother cell eventually releases the mature spore.
Slide 63. Faculty summary slide consolidates the spore-formation sequence.
Sporulation stepDeck sequence
1DNA replication / axial filament
2Asymmetric septum creates forespore + mother cell
3Mother cell engulfs forespore → second membrane
4Peptidoglycan layer develops between membranes
5Calcium added to spore core; maturation
6Mother cell releases mature spore
Handout-only clinical enrichment: endospores contain a protected core with dipicolinic acid and are built for survival, not reproduction. The handout emphasizes medically important spore formers in the Bacillus and Clostridium genera and uses reheated-rice Bacillus cereus food poisoning as a classic survival vignette.

Last 60 seconds
Gram+ = thick PG + teichoic acid. Gram- = thin PG + outer membrane/LPS/porins. Gram stain = CV → iodine → alcohol → safranin. FtsZ = division. NAG/NAM = peptidoglycan. Spores = extreme survival.
